newsitem.title: JAPAN: Property sales seen aiding M'bishi Trust long-term.
newsitem.headline: Property sales seen aiding M'bishi Trust long-term.

text.p: Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp's planned property sales, while cutting its expected profits this fiscal year, will have a positive effect on the bank's shares in the long-term, analysts said on Friday.
They added, however, that the announcement would do little to help the bank anytime soon, given the highly negative sentiment now gripping Japan's overall banking sector.
On Friday, Mitsubishi Trust said it had lowered its forecast of parent net profit in the year to March 31 to 85 billion yen from its earlier estimate of 150 billion yen.
This was due in part to plans to sell two properties, resulting in a special loss of 46.9 billion yen, in order to improve its asset quality and more effectively manage its property holdings.
"For Mitsubishi Trust, this is a good story as the unrealised losses on one of the two properties it's selling were a cause of concern," said Akira Takai, analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research Ltd.

He said the move showed that the bank was confident it could cut its problem loans to a manageable level in the current fiscal year and shoulder the resulting losses, and it should thus be viewed as a positive factor in the long term.
Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc, agreed.
"The decision is a welcome move. It seemed to me that Mitsubishi Trust is committed to improving its asset quality," he said.

A Mitsubishi Trust spokesman also said the bank has not changed its plans to dispose of 320 billion yen in problem loans in the current fiscal year despite the recent sharp declines in Tokyo stock prices.

He said the bank's latest earnings forecast included an appraisal loss of about 30 billion yen on its stock holdings, based on an assumption that the Nikkei average would end on March 31 at around 18,000, down from about 21,500 at the end of March 1996 but above Friday's close of 17,689.36.
Analysts said the size of the appraisal loss could change depending on the price of stocks the bank holds on March 31.
